project: Mycroft Phase 6 — Explainable Autonomous Monitoring Copilot

metadata.style_reference: mycroft_phase3_4k_9x16.mp4 — dark navy notebook cells, teal progress rule

numbers_policy: Every figure is quoted from the author's executed notebook run. The notebook was not re-run and the dataset is not in this package, so nothing was recomputed.
advisory: Research decision-support only. Agents prioritize evidence and anomalies; the human reviewer makes the final decision.

beats.title: Opening
beats.subtitle: Explainable Autonomous Monitoring
beats.narration: Hi, I am Dhrumil Shah, and this video is about Mycroft Phase 6, where I built an explainable autonomous monitoring copilot that runs five research agents over the market every day, scores what deserves a human look, and writes down exactly why.

beats.title: The problem
beats.subtitle: Too much to watch
beats.narration: Here is the problem. One analyst cannot watch a hundred and twenty names every day. Automate it and you get the opposite problem: a black box that says review this, with no reason attached. Neither one is usable.

beats.title: What is new
beats.subtitle: Auditable by construction
beats.narration: Phase 6 is the integration phase. Earlier phases each built one kind of signal. Phase 6 runs five of them together, combines them with weights you can read, and attaches a written reason to every single alert. Nothing is a black box.

beats.title: Architecture
beats.subtitle: Five agents, one queue
beats.narration: The shape is simple. The same market panel feeds five independent agents. Each raises its own flag. A transparent score adds those flags up. That produces a ranked review queue, an auditable event log, and two empty fields waiting for a human.

beats.title: Agent A
beats.subtitle: Robust anomaly detection
beats.narration: Agent A watches for abnormal days. It computes a rolling modified z-score on returns, volume and intraday range, built on medians rather than means, so a few wild days cannot hide the rest. Anything past four standard-equivalents is flagged.
beats.tts_text: Agent A watches for abnormal days. It computes a rolling modified z score on returns, volume and intraday range, built on medians rather than means, so a few wild days cannot hide the rest. Anything past four standard-equivalents is flagged.

beats.title: Agents B and C
beats.subtitle: Peers and risk
beats.narration: Agent B ranks each name inside its own industry, weighting weak momentum, high volatility and deep drawdown into a single peer-weakness number. Agent C scores risk across the whole market on the same day. Both fire in the worst twenty percent.

beats.title: Agent D
beats.subtitle: Thesis deterioration
beats.narration: Agent D carries the thesis-health idea forward from Phase 5. Five ranked components make a zero to one hundred score, and the agent fires when that score falls twenty points in twenty days. It is watching the change, not the level.

beats.title: Agent E
beats.subtitle: Unsupervised outliers
beats.narration: Agent E is the only machine-learning model here. An isolation forest, two hundred and fifty trees, fit on the training dates only, looks at eight features at once and finds the rows that do not look like anything else. It catches combinations the single-variable rules miss.

beats.title: Transparent scoring
beats.subtitle: Weights you can read
beats.narration: Now the part that makes it auditable. The priority is a plain sum. Two points for a robust anomaly, one for peer weakness, two for high risk, two for thesis deterioration, two for a multivariate outlier. No learned weights, no hidden model. Nine is the maximum.

beats.title: Explanations
beats.subtitle: Every alert carries its reason
beats.narration: And every flag writes its own reason, with the number that caused it. So the queue does not say review this. It says robust anomaly, z of seven point five, risk score point nine two, thesis down seventy-four points.
beats.tts_text: And every flag writes its own reason, with the number that caused it. So the queue does not say review this. It says robust anomaly, z of seven point five, risk score point nine two, thesis down seventy-four points.

beats.title: Monitoring summary
beats.subtitle: One day, in numbers
beats.narration: That produces a daily monitoring summary. On the eleventh of February, one hundred and twenty names monitored, forty-three flagged for review, and only three at priority five or above. Twenty-nine thesis deteriorations, fifteen high-risk names, eleven anomalies, four multivariate outliers.

beats.title: Queue and event log
beats.subtitle: Machine-readable, human-owned
beats.narration: The queue itself is short. S and P Global leads at priority eight, then Schwab at six, then UnitedHealth at five. Every row is also written to a JSON event log, with the agent outputs and two fields left deliberately empty: human decision, and human rationale.
beats.tts_text: The queue itself is short. S and P Global leads at priority eight, then Schwab at six, then United Health at five. Every row is also written to a JSON event log, with the agent outputs and two fields left deliberately empty: human decision, and human rationale.

beats.title: Honest diagnostic
beats.subtitle: Does the score mean anything?
beats.narration: So does the priority score actually mean anything? Measured over six years: at priority zero, large five-day moves happen eighteen percent of the time. At four, thirty-four. At six, thirty-nine. At eight, forty-one. The trend is real. But it is noisy, it dips at three, five and seven, and the high scores are rare. This is a historical diagnostic, not a forecast.

beats.title: Close
beats.subtitle: What I built
beats.narration: So, Phase 6. Five agents integrated into one monitoring pass. A transparent priority score. A written reason on every alert. An auditable JSON event log. And a human decision field that the system never fills in. Next comes scheduling it to run daily, calibrating the weights against outcomes, and a reviewer interface. Mycroft Project, Phase 6. Developed by Dhrumil Shah. Thank you for watching.
